# From S3 to traits {#sec-s3-traits}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

S3 is the object system most R code uses. A class is a string stored in an attribute, a generic is usually a function that calls `UseMethod()`, and a method is a function whose name joins the generic and the class with a dot. Nothing is declared ahead of time, and R finds the right method only when the generic is called. Rust's counterpart is the trait: a named set of methods that a type promises to provide. You declare the trait, implement it for each type, and the compiler checks every implementation and every call. This chapter turns the normal distribution from @sec-structs into the book's running class, written as an S3 class and as a Rust type that implements a `Distribution` trait, and then adds a second distribution to show what a shared interface buys. The matching section of the Rust book is "Defining Shared Behavior with Traits" [@rustbook, sec. 10.2].

## A normal distribution in S3

An S3 object is an ordinary R object with a `class` attribute. A constructor function builds the list and attaches the class:

```{r}
#| label: r-normal-class
normal <- function(mean = 0, sd = 1) {
  structure(list(mean = mean, sd = sd), class = "normal")
}

dist <- normal(0, 2)
class(dist)
unclass(dist)
```

Calling `unclass()` shows that underneath, `dist` is the same list as in @sec-structs. The class is a label on top of it.

In Rust, the struct from @sec-structs is already a type, so there's nothing to attach. The type `Normal` plays the role of the class.

## Generics and methods

In base R, `mean()` is already a generic, so supporting it takes one method, `mean.normal()`. A new generic, such as `variance()`, is a function that calls `UseMethod()`:

```{r}
#| label: r-generics
mean.normal <- function(x, ...) x$mean

variance <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("variance")
variance.normal <- function(x, ...) x$sd^2

mean(dist)
variance(dist)
```

In Rust, the methods are declared together in a trait, and an `impl` block provides them for one type:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-trait
trait Distribution {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64;
    fn variance(&self) -> f64;
}

struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

impl Distribution for Normal {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
        self.mean
    }

    fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
        self.sd * self.sd
    }
}

fn main() {
    let dist = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 2.0 };
    println!("{}", dist.mean());
    println!("{}", dist.variance());
}
```

The trait lists each method's signature and ends it with a semicolon instead of a body. The `impl Distribution for Normal` block then supplies the bodies, using the `&self` methods from @sec-structs. A struct can have a field and a method with the same name: `self.mean` is the field and `dist.mean()` is the method, much as `x$mean` and `mean(x)` are different things in R.

The pieces line up like this:

| S3 | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| A generic: `variance <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("variance")` | A method in a trait: `fn variance(&self) -> f64;` |
| A method: `variance.normal <- function(x, ...) ...` | An implementation: `impl Distribution for Normal { ... }` |
| A class: the string `"normal"` | A type: `Normal` |
| R finds the method when the generic is called | The compiler finds the implementation from the type |

A note on vocabulary: R calls `variance()` a generic, but in Rust "generic" means something else, a function or type with a type parameter (@sec-generics). This book uses "trait method" for the Rust side.

One difference isn't visible in the table. S3 generics are independent of each other, so a class can have a `mean()` method and no `variance()` method. A trait groups its methods, and an implementation has to supply every method the trait leaves without a body. In this trait, that's all of them.

## A second distribution

Here's a uniform distribution in S3, with the `variance()` method forgotten:

```{r}
#| label: r-uniform-incomplete
#| error: true
uniform <- function(min = 0, max = 1) {
  structure(list(min = min, max = max), class = "uniform")
}
mean.uniform <- function(x, ...) (x$min + x$max) / 2

u <- uniform(0, 6)
mean(u)
variance(u)
```

R accepted the class and its one method, and the gap only showed up when `variance(u)` ran. The same omission in Rust is a compile error, even though the program never calls `variance()`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-uniform-incomplete
#| error: true
trait Distribution {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64;
    fn variance(&self) -> f64;
}

struct Uniform {
    min: f64,
    max: f64,
}

impl Distribution for Uniform {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.min + self.max) / 2.0
    }
}

fn main() {
    let dist = Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 };
    println!("{}", dist.mean());
}
```

Implementing a trait is a promise to provide its methods, and the compiler holds you to the whole promise at once.

## Code that works with any distribution

The payoff of a shared interface is code that works with any type that provides it. In R, any function that calls generics works this way, because S3 dispatch happens inside each call:

```{r}
#| label: r-describe
variance.uniform <- function(x, ...) (x$max - x$min)^2 / 12

describe <- function(x) {
  cat("mean", mean(x), "variance", variance(x), "\n")
}

describe(normal(0, 2))
describe(uniform(0, 6))
```

In Rust, a function says in its signature that it accepts any type implementing `Distribution`. The trait and `Normal` are the same as before, compiled but not shown:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-describe
# trait Distribution {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64;
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64;
# }
#
# struct Normal {
#     mean: f64,
#     sd: f64,
# }
#
# impl Distribution for Normal {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
#         self.mean
#     }
#
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
#         self.sd * self.sd
#     }
# }
#
struct Uniform {
    min: f64,
    max: f64,
}

impl Distribution for Uniform {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.min + self.max) / 2.0
    }

    fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.max - self.min).powi(2) / 12.0
    }
}

fn describe(dist: impl Distribution) {
    println!("mean {}, variance {}", dist.mean(), dist.variance());
}

fn main() {
    describe(Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 2.0 });
    describe(Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 });
}
```

The `powi()` method raises a float to an integer power, so `powi(2)` is like `^2` in R. If you call `describe()` with a type that doesn't implement `Distribution`, the program doesn't compile, and the error lists the types that do.

This version of `describe()` takes its argument by value. A `Normal` stored in a variable and passed to it is *moved* into the function, and the variable can't be used afterward. @sec-ownership explains moves, and @sec-borrowing shows how a function can borrow a value instead.

::: {.callout-note title="Syntax ahead: impl Distribution"}
As an argument type, `impl Distribution` means "a value of any type that implements `Distribution`". It's the shortest way to write a generic function. @sec-generics covers the longer forms and how the compiler turns one generic function into code for each type.
:::

## Default methods

An S3 generic can have a `.default` method, which R uses when no method matches the class. Here it defines a standard deviation for anything that has a `variance()` method:

```{r}
#| label: r-default-method
std_dev <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("std_dev")
std_dev.default <- function(x, ...) sqrt(variance(x))

std_dev(normal(0, 2))
std_dev(uniform(0, 6))
```

A Rust trait can give a method a body, and every type that implements the trait gets that method without writing it:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-default-method
trait Distribution {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64;
    fn variance(&self) -> f64;

    fn std_dev(&self) -> f64 {
        self.variance().sqrt()
    }
}

# struct Normal {
#     mean: f64,
#     sd: f64,
# }
#
# impl Distribution for Normal {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
#         self.mean
#     }
#
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
#         self.sd * self.sd
#     }
# }
#
# struct Uniform {
#     min: f64,
#     max: f64,
# }
#
# impl Distribution for Uniform {
#     fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
#         (self.min + self.max) / 2.0
#     }
#
#     fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
#         (self.max - self.min).powi(2) / 12.0
#     }
# }
#
fn main() {
    let normal = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 2.0 };
    let uniform = Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 };
    println!("{}", normal.std_dev());
    println!("{}", uniform.std_dev());
}
```

The implementations of `Normal` and `Uniform` haven't changed, and both now have `std_dev()`. A type can still write its own version to replace the default; `Normal` could return `self.sd` directly. The standard library documentation lists each trait's methods under two headings: "Required Methods", the ones an implementation has to write, and "Provided Methods", the ones with a default body [@rust-std].

The uniform result also shows a difference in printing: R rounds to seven significant digits by default, while Rust prints every digit needed to identify the value (@sec-display).

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's default method applies to any object at all, not only to distributions:

```{r}
#| label: r-default-anything
#| error: true
std_dev("hello")
```

The call reaches `std_dev.default()` and fails one step later, inside `variance()`. A Rust default method exists only on types that implement the trait, so `std_dev()` can't be called on a string in the first place.
:::

## An S3 class is only a label

Because an S3 class is a string, you can attach it to anything:

```{r}
#| label: r-relabel
#| error: true
x <- "not a distribution"
class(x) <- "normal"
mean(x)
```

R dispatched to `mean.normal()`, which assumed a list and failed as soon as it used `x$mean`. Nothing in S3 connects the label to the data underneath. In Rust, a value's type is fixed when the value is created, so a string can't become a `Normal`.

## No inheritance

S3 classes can inherit. A class vector such as `c("normal", "distribution")` makes R look for a `normal` method first and a `distribution` method second, and `NextMethod()` passes a call along the chain. Rust has no inheritance between types. One struct can't extend another. Behavior that several types share goes in a trait, often as a default method like `std_dev()`, and data that several types share goes in a field that holds another struct. @sec-s4 returns to class hierarchies with S4's virtual classes.

::: {.callout-note title="Package developer notes: method registration and the orphan rule" collapse="true"}
A package registers its S3 methods with `S3method()` directives in its `NAMESPACE` file, and since R 3.6.0 it can register a method for a generic in another package, to take effect when that package is loaded [@r-exts, sec. 1.5.2]. In practice, any package can define a method for any generic and any class, including generics and classes it doesn't own.

Rust forbids that with the *orphan rule*: a crate can implement a trait for a type only if the crate defines the trait or the type. Implementing the standard library's `Display` trait for the standard library's `Vec<f64>` is a compile error. A type the crate defines also counts when it's the trait's type parameter, as in `impl Mul<Normal> for f64` (@sec-operators), though generic implementations have extra restrictions. The rule guarantees that two crates can never supply conflicting implementations of the same trait for the same type [@rustbook, sec. 10.2]. @sec-crates covers crates.
:::

## Summary

| R (S3) | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `structure(list(...), class = "normal")` | A struct type, `Normal` |
| A generic that calls `UseMethod()` | A method declared in a trait |
| A method such as `variance.normal()` | `impl Distribution for Normal` |
| A call with no applicable method fails at runtime | A missing required method fails to compile |
| Any function can call any generic | `fn describe(dist: impl Distribution)` |
| A `.default` method covers any class without its own method | A default method exists only for implementors |
| `class(x) <-` relabels any object | A value's type can't change |
| Class vectors and `NextMethod()` | No inheritance; traits and composition instead |
| Any package can register any method | The orphan rule |
